title: Jeju Island: Why First-Timers Need at Least 2 Nights, 3 Days
html:
If you only have one free day on your Korea trip, Jeju Island is probably not worth the trip. But if you can spare 2 nights, 3 days, it's one of the best side trips you can take from Seoul. Jeju is a volcanic island about an hour's flight south of the mainland, with beaches, a huge dormant volcano, lava tube caves, and a completely different, slower pace than Seoul.

This guide is for first-timers who have never been to Jeju (or Korea) before. It covers how to get there, how to get around once you land, and a simple 2N3D (2 nights, 3 days — that's how Koreans write "2 nights, 3 days" trips) plan that hits the highlights without rushing.

Getting to Jeju: Flights from Seoul

There's no bridge or tunnel to Jeju, so unless you're taking a long overnight ferry from a mainland port, you'll fly. Flights leave from Gimpo Airport (김포공항, Seoul's smaller airport, mostly used for domestic flights — not Incheon International, which is for flights from outside Korea) and take about 1 hour. It's one of the busiest short-haul routes in the world, with flights departing every 15–30 minutes for most of the day on Korean Air, Asiana, Jeju Air, Jin Air, T'way, and Air Busan.

One-way fares are usually somewhere around ₩30,000–80,000 (roughly $22–60) if you book ahead, but they climb fast closer to the flight date — sometimes 2–3x higher. Book through the airline's own site or a Korean site like Naver Flight for the best prices; international booking sites don't always show the cheapest budget-airline fares. A real tip from locals: many Koreans flying Seoul–Jeju fly the very first or very last flight of the day, since those are usually the cheapest and least crowded.


Photo: Masakatsu Ukon, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Once you land, you'll need a way to get around — Jeju doesn't have a subway. Most first-timers either rent a car (the easiest way to reach the more remote spots in this guide) or rely on intercity buses, which are cheap but slower. If you don't have an International Driving Permit, stick to buses and taxis — Korea requires one to drive, your home license alone isn't enough.

Day 1: Seongsan Ilchulbong, the Sunrise Peak

Seongsan Ilchulbong is a volcanic crater that rises straight out of the ocean on Jeju's east coast — its name literally means "Sunrise Peak." It's one of Jeju's most photographed spots and a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site, so it's a great first stop after landing.

The walk up to the crater rim takes about 30–40 minutes on a paved path and isn't too strenuous, though it can get steep near the top. Admission is a small fee (last checked, around ₩5,000 for adults, less for children/teens — prices can change, so check the Visit Jeju site before you go). The lower coastal walking trail around the base is free. The site closes on the first Monday of each month for maintenance, so avoid planning your trip around that day.


Photo: Yoo Chung, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Go early in the morning if you can — not just for the "sunrise peak" name, but because tour buses arrive in waves from mid-morning, and the paved path can get crowded. If you're staying near the east coast overnight, catching an actual sunrise from the base area is a nice, free bonus.

Day 1 or 2: A Side Trip to Udo Island

Right next to Seongsan is Udo ("cow island" — the island looks like a lying-down cow from certain angles), a small island you reach by a short ferry ride from Seongsan's harbor. Most people rent a bike, scooter, or small electric car for a few hours to loop around the island's beaches and sea cliffs — it's small enough to see in half a day.

Udo is known for its unusually clear turquoise water and black-sand and white coral-sand beaches. It's also famous on Jeju for peanut ice cream (made from Udo's own peanut crop) — worth trying while you're there. Bring the ferry terminal's posted schedule in mind, since the last boat back to Jeju's mainland isn't too late in the evening.


Photo: Jeju Film Commission, Korea Open Government License Type I, via Wikimedia Commons

Day 2: Hallasan, South Korea's Highest Mountain

Hallasan is a huge shield volcano that makes up most of Jeju Island, and at around 1,947 meters, it's the tallest peak in South Korea. At the very top is a crater lake called Baengnokdam. Reaching the summit is a full-day hike (figure 8–10 hours round trip), so this is only for travelers who are reasonably fit and have the time — most first-timers on a 2N3D trip instead hike partway up one of the lower, shorter trails for the views, which is a perfectly good way to experience the mountain.


Photo: Yoo Chung, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

Important if you do want the summit: the two trails that reach Baengnokdam (Seongpanak and Gwaneumsa) require a free advance reservation through Jeju National Park's own booking site — you can be turned away at the trailhead without one. Reservations tend to open about a month ahead and fill up fast in peak seasons (October, and late March–April). There are also seasonal entry cutoff times — in colder months, you may need to start the summit trails by late morning to be allowed in at all. Rules like this change by season, so double-check the official Hallasan National Park site a few days before you go, not just when you book flights.

Day 2 or 3: Manjanggul Cave, a Lava Tube You Can Walk Through

Jeju was formed by volcanic eruptions, and Manjanggul is one of the results: a long lava tube (a tunnel-like cave formed by flowing lava) that you can walk into. Only about 1 kilometer of the cave is open to visitors, but it's an easy, flat walk — no climbing involved — and a nice contrast to a day of hiking and beaches.


Photo: Gary Cycles, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

It's cool and a little damp inside year-round (a nice break if you're visiting in Jeju's humid summer), so bring a light layer even in warm weather. Good, grippy shoes help — the cave floor is uneven rock in places. This is an easy stop to fit in on your way to or from the airport on your last day, since it's in the island's north.

Flight vs. Ferry, and Getting Around Once You're There

Here's a quick comparison for the two decisions every first-timer has to make on a Jeju trip — how to get there, and how to get around once they land:

OptionTimeRough CostBest for
Flight (from Gimpo)~1 hour₩30,000–80,000+Almost everyone — it's faster and often cheaper than the ferry once you add up time
Overnight ferry (from mainland ports)~5–13 hoursVaries by route/cabin classTravelers bringing a car over, or who want the slow-travel experience
Rental car (on Jeju)—Daily rental fee + fuelReaching Hallasan, Manjanggul, and other spots off the bus routes — requires an International Driving Permit
Intercity bus (on Jeju)Slower, depends on routeA few thousand won per rideBudget travelers without a driving permit, sticking to well-connected towns
TaxiFastest point-to-pointHigher for longer, cross-island tripsShort hops or whenever a bus route doesn't go where you need

💬 Planning a Jeju trip and not sure it fits your itinerary? Drop your question in the comments — happy to help you work out the details!
meta_description: A beginner's guide to Jeju Island: how to fly from Seoul, what to see in a 2-night, 3-day trip, and why a day trip isn't enough.
